claims.claim: Present value is the current worth of money promised in the future, discounted at a rate; OpenStax's Principles of Finance states it as the value today of tomorrow's cash flow.
A given amount of money is worth more today than the same amount at a future date, because money in hand today can be invested or deposited to earn a return while waiting.
Discounting is the reverse of growth: it lowers a future value back to the current period, while compounding carries a present value forward to the future.
The present value formula is PV = FV × 1/(1 + r)^n, derived by reversing FV = PV × (1 + r)^n; with annual compounding this is PV = FV ÷ (1 + rate)^years.
The discount rate is the rate used to determine the present value of a future cash flow; OpenStax calls it the annual rate of reduction on a future value and the inverse of the growth rate.
With a positive rate, the present value of a future amount is always less than the future value (unless the rate is negative), which serves as a check on calculations.
Original worked example (arithmetic verified): $110.25 received in 2 years at 5% is worth $100 today, because 1.05 × 1.05 = 1.1025 and 110.25 ÷ 1.1025 = 100.00.

Present value is used to compare money at different times: saving toward a future goal (college, retirement), judging loan repayments in today's dollars, and business decisions about new products, equipment, and facilities.
The honest framing: present value converts a future amount into today's terms for comparison; the future amount itself is not changed, and the result depends on the discount rate chosen.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sources phrase the present value definition with different emphasis.
positions: OpenStax Principles of Finance: present value is the value today of tomorrow's cash flow, tied to the discount rate.
Investopedia: present value is the amount a future sum of money is worth today given a specified rate of return.
CFI: money in the present is worth more than the same sum of money promised in the future.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: All three agree on the substance — current worth of a future amount at a rate. The lesson teaches the OpenStax working definition and attributes it, with CFI and Investopedia as corroboration.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Formula presentation differs between a simple single division and a compounding-frequency form.
positions: CFI: PV = FV / (1 + (i/m))^(m×t), with m compounding periods per year.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: For annual compounding — the literacy level of this lesson — both reduce to PV = FV ÷ (1 + rate)^years. The lesson states the simple form and uses only annual compounding.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Finance, Section 7.1: Now versus Later Concepts
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Internet Archive capture (2022-09-30 snapshot) on 2026-08-21 because openstax.org blocks scripted fetches. Supports: the time value of money rests on the fact that cash can earn interest income while invested; it is better to be paid today, or you lose out on the interest you would have earned; a lump sum is a one-time cash flow at a single point in time and the basis for all other cash flows. Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Finance, Section 7.3: Methods for Solving Time Value of Money Problems
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Internet Archive capture (2022-09-30 snapshot) on 2026-08-21. Supports: solving for present value is the exact opposite of solving for future value; with a positive rate the present value is always less than the future value unless the rate is negative; the 5% growth series $100 → $105 (year 1) → $110.25 (year 2) → $115.76 (year 3) → $121.55 (year 4) → $127.63 (year 5); a $50,000 lump sum five years from now at 5% has a present value of $39,176.31. The lesson's worked example ($110.25 in 2 years at 5% = $100 today) reverses the book's own year-two growth value; arithmetic independently computed. Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Finance, Section 7.4: Applications of TVM in Finance
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Internet Archive capture (2022-09-30 snapshot) on 2026-08-21. Supports: to find a present value we reverse the growth concept and discount the future value back to the current period; the discount rate is the interest rate used to determine the present value of a future cash flow — the annual rate of reduction on a future value and the inverse of the growth rate; present value as 'the value today of tomorrow's cash flow'; PV = FV × 1/(1 + r)^n derived from FV = PV × (1 + r)^n; compounding moves present value forward while discounting equates a future value to present dollars; personal applications (college fund, retirement savings); a $20,000 goal one year out at 5% needs $19,047.62 today; a 30-year $1,000 savings bond at 5% costs $231.38. Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Time Value of Money
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Supports: a dollar today is worth more than the same dollar promised later, because money in hand can be invested to earn a return (and future money carries the risk that it may never be received); the present value calculation divides the future value by the growth factor (worked example PV = $1,100 / (1 + 5%)^1 ≈ $1,047.62); companies apply the time value of money to decisions about new product development, acquiring new business equipment or facilities, and establishing credit terms. Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Present Value - PV
sourceRecords.notes: The live page is JavaScript-walled; read a 2006 Internet Archive capture of the dictionary entry on 2026-08-21 (canonical URL registered). Supports the evergreen working definition: present value is the amount a future sum of money is worth today given a specified rate of return, with the classic example that $620 today is worth $1,000 in five years at 10%. Definitional corroboration only; the lesson's teaching, formula, and examples come from OpenStax and CFI.
